scope: All 192 original Science drills, 80 held-out Science questions and 72 held-out Reading questions; every complete shared passage was read alongside its questions. The separately reviewed 11 new Science transfer questions and 144 new Reading drills are outside this legacy review.
reviewMethod: Check each keyed answer against the full passage, table, graph or model, including units and comparison denominators.
Check each wrong choice for alternate validity, unsupported inference or a missing condition.
Keep every historical ID, answer index and correct-answer text stable; strengthen incorrect alternatives and explanations without changing the assessed concept.
Replace generic Reading explanation endings with source-specific evidence and reasons the competing choices fail.
Review revised options again for overlap; several draft alternatives were discarded because they were paraphrases of the key.

defectsRepaired.repair: The competing chair-count option now asks about a before/after occupancy comparison the table directly measures.

defectsRepaired.problem: Both normal/normal cues and both east/east cues fail to distinguish the scientists.
defectsRepaired.repair: All three distractors now rotate one cue at a time, giving different predictions; the keyed joint rotation remains the sole nonseparating design.

defectsRepaired.problem: Three individually valid rows competed with the all-three answer.
defectsRepaired.repair: The task explicitly asks for all fitting rows and the partial alternatives say only.

defectsRepaired.problem: Droplet contribution could also be inferred from the both-removed treatment combined with the solids-removed result.
defectsRepaired.repair: The task explicitly asks for a comparison retaining solid ash, separating the intended single-factor test.

defectsRepaired.problem: The explanation said the first two choices matched even though the second was outside range.
defectsRepaired.repair: Name the actual fitting force/extension pairs and distinguish the out-of-range measurement.

defectsRepaired.problem: The explanation referred to the second choice for a root-length claim now in the first choice.
defectsRepaired.repair: Name the claim and the actual low-salt counterexamples without a positional reference.

defectsRepaired.problem: The context did not state whether 12 insects were individual temperature units or one shared arena.
defectsRepaired.repair: Specify individual testing and independently maintained arenas, making the biological replication claim valid.

defectsRepaired.problem: The narrator’s aunt was described once as our aunt even though the cellist is not identified as a relative.
defectsRepaired.repair: Use my aunt consistently across all copies of the shared passage.

limits: This is an authored correctness and teaching-quality review, not a blind psychometric study or a guarantee of a 36.
Held-out Reading forms still use similar themes about interpretation and evidence; raw accuracy on them is not an official scaled ACT score.

items.answerText: To check how consistently each condition reached the endpoint

Replication alone does not separate mass from surface area; that depends on the large-piece/crushed-piece comparison at equal mass. A common systematic stopwatch bias can persist in every replicate, and the gas endpoint must still be defined.

items.answerText: Gas collection fell to 0.3 mL/h when microbes were removed and rose to 5.7 mL/h when they were restored.

items.answerText: The collected gas contains methane.

items.answerText: The removal result would be less able to distinguish the scientists because two factors had changed.

items.answerText: Organisms use oxygen while light-dependent photosynthesis is absent.
items.reviewedEvidence: R’s mechanism is continued respiration without photosynthesis. That can account for the measured fall from 9 to 5 mg/L even while cooler water’s equilibrium oxygen capacity increases.

items.answerText: Both proposed routes can preserve viability, but the tests do not identify the actual route.

A five-point laboratory difference does not identify the route that occurred: route frequency and real transport were not observed. Ten viable seawater-treated seeds also do not rule out that route. Feasibility is different from historical identification.

items.answerText: Mass of water absorbed by seeds at each concentration before germination

Root length samples only successful seedlings; residual pad salt is not seed water uptake; dry mass deliberately excludes the water the mechanism concerns. The measurement tests a prediction but would not by itself prove the whole causal chain.
Liquid V’s row gives 0.20 mm/s in the r = 0.4 mm column. The 0.05 mm/s entry is for the smaller 0.2 mm bead.
The radius term is squared: (2r)²/r² = 4. In U, doubling radius from 0.2 to 0.4 mm increases speed from 0.2 to 0.8 mm/s, a factor of 4.
At the same 0.4 mm radius, U has viscosity 1 and speed 0.8 mm/s. Doubling viscosity halves the model’s speed, giving 0.4 mm/s.

items.answerText: To keep the density difference between bead and liquid from changing along with viscosity
items.reviewedEvidence: With bead material fixed, equal liquid density keeps the bead–liquid density difference constant, leaving viscosity as the liquid property being compared. Equal density does not make viscosities or radii equal, and an equal travel distance does not guarantee equal speed.

items.answerText: A 0.4 mm bead moves at 0.8 mm/s in V.
items.reviewedEvidence: A 0.4 mm bead in V should move at 0.2 mm/s, one-fourth its speed in U because V’s viscosity is four times larger. A repeat value of 0.8 contradicts this inverse-viscosity prediction. The other listed values match the data/model.

items.answerText: Use a liquid denser than the bead.
items.reviewedEvidence: Direction depends on the bead–liquid density relationship: a bead less dense than the surrounding liquid tends to rise, so a liquid denser than the bead reverses the original direction. Changing viscosity or bead size can change speed; release depth changes travel conditions. None of those three changes reverses the stated density relationship.

items.answerText: Newly ejected fragments become less abundant with distance.

items.answerText: Shock-deformed quartz is present in samples 20 and 100 m outside the rim.

items.answerText: The glass alone would not distinguish the three explanations.
items.reviewedEvidence: The key restriction is preexisting: all three scientists explicitly allow preexisting volcanic glass in this basalt landscape. Its presence supplies neither an event date nor proof of shock heating, and D is not the only viewpoint that permits old material. This observation alone cannot separate the three mechanisms.

items.answerText: It would support the interpretation that the 20 m fragment abundance exceeds ordinary background.
items.reviewedEvidence: Compare the same units: 4 kg/m² at 20 m is twenty times the 0.2 kg/m² control background. This strengthens the claim of unusual near-rim accumulation. The 300 m sample equals background, not the 20 m sample; the control does not by itself identify impact, steam explosion, or dissolution as the cause.

items.answerText: To prevent expectations about distance from influencing grain classification
items.reviewedEvidence: A classifier who expects more shock grains near the rim could unconsciously classify borderline grains differently. Hiding distance reduces that expectation bias. It does not make collection distances equal, control the physical proportion of grains, or replace a background sample.

items.answerText: A freshly exposed layer demonstrably deposited by the pit-forming event contains shock-deformed quartz.
items.reviewedEvidence: D permits groundwater dissolution, ordinary background fragments, and old glass, but predicts no shock-deformed quartz from the pit-forming collapse. Tying shock grains to a layer demonstrably deposited by that event directly contradicts D; merely finding old or ordinary material would not.

More concentration decimals improve a different precision; a greater separation may change the lag but does not improve sampling time resolution; later observations do not refine the already passed peaks.

S has 50 survivors from 1,000 initial viable cells. 50/1,000 × 100 = 5%. R’s 850 survivors correspond to 85%, not S’s value.
The mixed culture would have 50 S and 850 R survivors, or 900 total. R’s share is 850/900 × 100 ≈ 94%. The 85% value is R’s survival fraction within its own initial population.

items.answerText: To count cells able to form colonies after the specified 1 h exposure without continuing the treatment

Cells lost while growing on compound-containing agar could reflect further inhibition, not just survival of the one-hour exposure. Removing the compound does not undo earlier deaths, equalize colony starting counts, or turn this into a growth-rate comparison.

items.answerText: R cells survived the tested compound concentrations better than S cells.
items.reviewedEvidence: Equal starting counts make survival comparable: R has 900 versus 350 survivors at 1 µg/mL and 850 versus 50 at 4 µg/mL. R’s survival is not constant across doses. No reproduction-rate or DNA/mutation measurement identifies why the strains differ, so neither faster growth nor induced mutation follows.

items.answerText: Both counts double while the R fraction remains about 94%.
items.reviewedEvidence: One division per survivor multiplies each strain by two: S 50→100 and R 850→1,700. The total is 1,800, and 1,700/1,800 equals 850/900, about 94%. Equal multiplicative growth preserves the fraction; it neither doubles only one strain nor adds the same absolute count to both.

D says water absorption is not required, not that water can never coexist with a dust avalanche, so its presence alone does not exclude D.

items.answerText: Far-red
items.reviewedEvidence: Far-red at 750 nm has 10% absorption, below green’s 20%, red’s 80%, and blue’s 85%.

items.answerText: 8 µmol/min
items.reviewedEvidence: Net red oxygen is 7 µmol/min. Adding the assumed 1 µmol/min consumed by respiration gives gross production of 8.

items.answerText: To compare wavelength effects without also changing the number of supplied photons per second
items.reviewedEvidence: Equal incident photon rate holds supplied photon number per second fixed, isolating wavelength from that input. Different absorption fractions still mean different absorbed photon rates; photon energy changes with wavelength; and oxygen production is the response, not a controlled quantity.

items.answerText: Every additional 100 nm in wavelength always increases net oxygen.
items.reviewedEvidence: Net oxygen falls from 8 at 450 nm to 1 at 550, rises to 7 at 650, then falls to 0 at 750. It does not increase monotonically with wavelength.

items.answerText: Gross production is 1 µmol/min, equal to consumption.
items.reviewedEvidence: Use the stated mass balance: net = gross − respiration. With net 0 and respiration fixed at 1 µmol/min, gross must also be 1. A zero net change does not mean no processes occur; 0.5/0.5 violates the given respiration rate, and 0/1 would give −1 net.

items.answerText: Wavelength and absorption differ together, and no independent absorption manipulation was made.
items.reviewedEvidence: Wavelength and absorption percentage vary together, so the table cannot assign all wavelength effects specifically to absorption. An independent absorption manipulation at fixed wavelength would help separate those factors. Equal area and a dark respiration comparison are controls; a red/blue response difference by itself does not distinguish the proposed causal routes.

items.answerText: 1.5 mm
items.reviewedEvidence: 30 N is halfway between loading points 20 N (1 mm) and 40 N (2 mm), giving 1.5 mm. Use the loading, not unloading, curve.

items.answerText: 40–60 N increases extension by 2 mm.
items.reviewedEvidence: The first two 20 N increments each add 1 mm, but the next adds 2. A constant extension/force proportionality over the whole range would require equal rises for equal force steps.

items.answerText: 1 mm
items.reviewedEvidence: The unloading curve has 1 mm extension at zero force, compared with the original 0 mm. The remaining 1 mm is unrecovered, permanent deformation.

items.answerText: It is 1 mm greater.
items.reviewedEvidence: Loading at 40 N is 2 mm; unloading at 40 N is 3 mm. Unloading exceeds loading by 1 mm.

items.answerText: No; the unloading trial began at 60 N, not 80 N.
items.reviewedEvidence: Residual extension must be read after unloading from the specified maximum load. The only unloading curve begins at 60 N and ends at 1 mm, while the 80 N point is still loaded. No rule makes residual deformation proportional to maximum force or constant above 60 N, so none supplies the unmeasured unloading-from-80 result.

items.answerText: 30°C/20 mL versus 30°C/50 mL
items.reviewedEvidence: To isolate water, hold temperature at the requested 30°C and compare 20 with 50 mL: CO₂ is 55 versus 100 mg. Changing temperature as well confounds the comparison. Sterile versus nonsterile changes microbial status, and two 50 mL treatments test temperature rather than water.

items.answerText: 40 mg
items.reviewedEvidence: The 50 mL conditions produce 60 mg at 15°C and 100 at 30°C. The increase is 100−60 = 40 mg.

items.answerText: At 30°C the increase is 45 mg.
items.reviewedEvidence: At 30°C CO₂ rises from 55 to 100 mg, an increase of 45 rather than 30. The water effect therefore differs across the two tested temperatures.

items.answerText: Some carbon originally in organic material can leave the material as CO₂.
items.reviewedEvidence: Decomposition can transfer existing organic carbon into CO₂ without creating carbon atoms. The soil also contains possible carbon sources, so the experiment does not trace every CO₂ atom specifically to the added litter. CO₂ mass alone does not give total litter mass loss because composition, other products, and final litter mass were not measured.

items.answerText: The exact fraction of the original litter mass lost in each treatment is known.
items.reviewedEvidence: The study measures cumulative CO₂, not final litter mass, and supplies no conversion of litter composition to mass loss. It cannot determine exact litter fraction lost from those measurements alone.

items.answerText: dismissing a customary signal to recognizing its varied roles without declaring it universally necessary
items.reviewedEvidence: Build the change from the beginning and ending, not one incident. In paragraph 1 the narrator treats the bell as neglected obsolete equipment. By paragraphs 6–8, the narrator asks about both supported routines and disturbance, and declines to interpret the worker’s pause with certainty. Ada adds meaning rather than replacing the records; the complaints remain valid; modern navigation is not shown to depend on the bell.

items.answerText: Includes it in the repair description
items.reviewedEvidence: Locate the copying action in paragraph 3: because the spreadsheet has no field for Ada, the narrator puts her name in the description. The absence of a field does not prompt a redesign or deletion. The later notebook records observed gestures, and Ada’s asking about the silence does not make her the cable repairer.

items.answerText: temporarily silencing the bell
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 6 names the proposed intervention: silencing the bell “during a trial period.” The complaints explain why, but no changed hour, vessel-only schedule, or loudness study is proposed. Keep the actual council action separate from plausible alternatives to it.

items.answerText: can value the bell’s meanings while still supporting a test of the complaints about it
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 7 combines two facts: the father voted for the trial, and he wants the council to ask useful questions about the bell. He can recognize its varied meanings and take complaints seriously. The revision does not oppose a trial, he no longer treats navigation as its only function, and the final sentence accepts different meanings rather than demanding agreement.

items.answerText: no longer needed for its original practical purpose
items.reviewedEvidence: Substitute the definition into paragraph 7: the bell is an instruction left over from navigation whose original warning function has been superseded by lights. “No longer needed for its original practical purpose” fits. The word does not mean damaged, unfamiliar, or merely inherited; something inherited can still perform a current practical function.

items.answerText: presenting an emotionally significant habit as part of ordinary daily life
items.reviewedEvidence: In paragraph 4, Ada connects the bell to her husband and her continued kettle routine while counting a customer’s change. The ordinary manner and emotionally significant content coexist. She does not ask for commemoration, supply the repair date, or imply that the habit has become meaningless. The detail works through understatement, not an explicit appeal.

items.answerText: a practical counterweight to the narrator’s growing emotional investment
items.reviewedEvidence: The warning is to finish the spreadsheet instead of writing a sentimental essay. It checks the narrator’s emotional investment against the job’s practical task. The clerk does not challenge copied dates or propose replacing records with stories. Her later suggestion of a note leaves room for uncertainty without making the spreadsheet a residents’ survey.

items.answerText: The revision narrows a sweeping claim while keeping the underlying question about the bell’s value
items.reviewedEvidence: Compare what is removed with what remains. The first draft turns Ada’s story into a claim that everyone needs the bell. The revision still asks about its value but includes both supported routines and the people disturbed. It introduces neither cost evidence nor a no-trial decision, and it moves away from making Ada represent everybody.

items.answerText: The risk of assigning a broad meaning to an observation without sufficient evidence
items.reviewedEvidence: The final pause could mean listening or resting. This directly repeats paragraph 5’s caution that looking up could have several explanations, and paragraph 6’s refusal to turn Ada’s routine into a universal claim. Recordkeeping and family disagreement are related themes, but they do not explain the narrator’s refusal to assign a meaning to this particular gesture.

items.answerText: interpret an encouraging count in terms of its definition, the library’s goals, and the study’s limits
items.reviewedEvidence: Follow the librarian’s recurring distinction between a measure and the question it answers (paragraphs 2 and 6). Occupancy can inform a goal about providing space without counting distinct people. Cards illustrate possible uses without replacing counts. Additional observations help, but the argument does not promise that repetition removes every outside influence or permits estimating new visitors from chairs alone.

items.answerText: How many distinct people used the library
items.reviewedEvidence: One occupied seat at noon is not an identified visitor: the same person might still occupy it at four, or several people might use it at different times. Paragraph 2 explicitly excludes distinct visitors from the measure. The table does provide occupied-seat snapshots, time-of-day comparisons, and before/after afternoon averages. All three alternatives are quantities the counts actually support.

items.answerText: To allow uses the designers had not anticipated to be described
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 3 says the open line permits an answer the designers had not anticipated. Bus-watching illustrates the benefit. Restricting answers to the observation categories would defeat that purpose; the passage does not describe matching individuals to cards or using the card to seek agreement with staff.

items.answerText: values newly noticed uses while avoiding a claim that those uses characterize all visitors
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 4 accepts bus watching as an overlooked use while warning that a handful of comments cannot show how common it is. The librarian neither selects it as the cause of the whole increase nor requires a new survey before mentioning it. Offering a voluntary card also does not establish that its respondents represent all visitors.

items.answerText: held constant or accounted for in the comparison
items.reviewedEvidence: In paragraph 5, examinations and a rainy week are conditions that changed between months and were not held constant or accounted for in a controlled comparison. Counting times and checking records are procedures, not the meaning of “controlled” here. The word also does not refer to selecting card respondents.

items.answerText: show that a measurement must match the question being asked
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 6 gives two different goals: providing space and attracting additional people. Occupied seats address the first; distinct-visitor counts address the second. A more precise count of the wrong quantity still does not answer the other question. The contrast neither dismisses numbers in favor of stories nor limits the report to finance.

items.answerText: the value of clear scope over a more evocative but less specific phrase
items.reviewedEvidence: In paragraph 8, the librarian rejects the evocative phrase as the report heading and chooses a title naming weekday occupancy before and after opening. That title communicates both topic and scope. It does not conceal interpretation until an experiment, exclude the visitor comments, or privilege persuasion over an accurate account of the evidence.

items.answerText: The observed afternoon occupancy increased more than the observed noon occupancy
items.reviewedEvidence: Compute changes in the same units: afternoon 17 − 8 = 9 occupied seats, noon 8 − 6 = 2. The afternoon increase is larger in both count and proportion. Nine is not the eight chairs added; movement into the retained seats can also change occupancy. After opening, 17 afternoon seats exceeds 8 noon seats.

items.answerText: Seat occupancy rose at the observed times, but these numbers alone do not establish an increase in distinct visitors
items.reviewedEvidence: The table shows more occupied seats at each observed time, and paragraph 2 explains why this does not identify additional individuals. Fixed observation locations aid comparison but do not isolate cause. Missing other times does not turn occupancy into a lower bound on new visitors, and voluntary comments do not establish how common each activity is.

items.answerText: how researchers can use archives while making the limits of recorded evidence visible
items.reviewedEvidence: Both writers want sources used with their limits visible. Passage A places recollections beside plans without blending them into a seamless account; Passage B documents how records and interviews were created. Neither promises that oral accounts complete the story, makes private voices unnecessary, or assumes every gap was deliberate exclusion.

items.answerText: decisions an institution needed to record
items.reviewedEvidence: Passage A, paragraph 1 explicitly says the archive was organized around the decisions an institution needed to record. Petitions contain some resident names, but that does not make residents’ experiences the collection’s organizing purpose. Interviews and the comparison of sources belong to the historian’s later research, not the original collection.

items.answerText: Who was invited to speak
items.reviewedEvidence: Passage B, paragraph 7 lists invitation, refusal, and interview questions as conditions that should travel with oral-history evidence. “Who was invited to speak” is one of those explicit questions. Agreement with minutes, uninterrupted delivery, and selecting representative interviews are plausible research concerns, but none is the specific documentation the paragraph recommends.

items.answerText: wants differences in evidence sources to remain apparent to readers
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 4 explains the interruptions as marks of movement between different kinds of evidence. Keeping them visible allows readers to judge each source and the limits of conclusions requiring both. The choice does not rank recollections above plans, establish design changes, or imply that one source must contain the whole event.

items.answerText: understandable
items.reviewedEvidence: The sentence concerns making the archive’s limits understandable. A limit can be explained even when the missing conversation cannot be reconstructed and the sources do not settle the whole question. “Complete,” “consistent,” and “recoverable” would change the archivist’s restrained goal rather than paraphrase “intelligible.”

items.answerText: illustrate aspects of a project that engineering plans do not fully describe
items.reviewedEvidence: The household details in paragraph 3 add dimensions of lived experience—washing, shopping paths, and work noise—to the same project described in engineering records. The historian explicitly says they do not invalidate the plans. They do not date construction more precisely, establish what the council foresaw, or determine structural dimensions.

items.answerText: challenges the assumption that every past experience originally produced a document
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 5 locates some absences before preservation: the activity was never recorded, not necessarily lost or discarded. Thus an event need not have generated a document. This distinction does not deny that undescribed records are evidence, identify deliberate disposal as the main cause, or prescribe a new arrangement for oral histories.

items.answerText: Adding personal accounts can broaden understanding without making the evidence complete
items.reviewedEvidence: Pair Passage A’s “adding voices” does not fill every silence (paragraph 3) with Passage B’s warning that expanded collections can still create an illusion of completeness (paragraph 7). Both support broadening evidence while keeping limits. Neither makes interviews a prerequisite for useful records, limits interviews to checking officials, or favors hiding source boundaries.

items.answerText: Passage A emphasizes composing a historical account; Passage B emphasizes describing how collections and new records are made
items.reviewedEvidence: Passage A follows a historian choosing and presenting evidence in a chapter about a bridge. Passage B examines collection formation, institutional categories, and documenting new interviews. Both discuss memory and support private voices. Neither treats institutional categories as natural truth or argues that adding personal material weakens an archive.

items.answerText: revises an appealing prediction after recognizing spatial, temporal, and causal limits in its data
items.reviewedEvidence: The sequence expands what is measured, confronts recovery over time, and limits the claim about barriers. The team revises the attractive initial forecast rather than merely making it more precise or confirming it. Paragraph 5 rejects ever smaller groups as automatic evidence, and paragraph 6 leaves the barriers’ causal role unresolved.

items.answerText: Sand was removed from one section and deposited farther along the shore
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 2 describes the fifth-week storm redistributing sand: removal from one section and deposition farther along the shore. The calmer-weather return occurs later in paragraph 4. Neither uniform loss at every point nor a barrier-specific accumulation is reported for this storm. Track the event and its timing separately from later interpretations.

items.answerText: A broader change in beach volume
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 3 adds spatial information—more measurement points and distances between them—to estimate a broader volume change. That is different from assuming a permanent loss rate, tracing sand to particular winds, or isolating barriers’ effects. The expanded survey improves the quantity estimated while leaving temporal and causal limits.

items.answerText: consider the correction of assumptions part of explaining their findings
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 7 keeps the graph with a note identifying the assumptions that exceeded the observations. This exposes how the interpretation changed. The original four observations remain valid; what failed was extrapolating them. The revised account is explicitly readable without being final, so retaining the graph is neither distrust of early data nor a contest between certain forecasts.

items.answerText: open to revision in light of further evidence
items.reviewedEvidence: The supervisor glosses “a provisional account” as a model compared with new conditions rather than protected from them. The issue is revisability in light of evidence, not whether the account is public, purely theoretical, or geographically restricted. Substitute the definition into the sentence and check that it preserves this relation to future tests.

items.answerText: a practical causal question that the existing comparisons cannot fully answer
items.reviewedEvidence: The visitors ask whether the barriers are saving the beach—a question about cause. Paragraph 6 explains that different weather in the before/after periods prevents attributing the change to barriers alone. Equal period lengths and locations of gains would supply useful descriptions, but neither is the question’s main function in the argument.

items.answerText: continuing a testable investigation rather than preserving a fixed prediction
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 8 removes physical stakes but retains coordinate references, observations, definitions, and questions for another group. Continuity makes further testing possible while leaving the prediction open. The passage does not assess whether stakes moved sand, give a fixed forecast as a standard, or ask successors to discard the survey locations.

items.answerText: Sand can move among locations and return over time, so a short decline at one point need not describe permanent beach-wide loss
items.reviewedEvidence: Combine two distinct limits: the storm redistributes sand among locations (paragraph 2), and later calm waves return some of it (paragraph 4). A local early decline therefore need not be permanent beach-wide loss. Nothing establishes equal opposing amounts, exact between-visit movements, or a barrier-caused recovery.

items.answerText: Both favor information and assumptions that can be tested as conditions change
items.reviewedEvidence: A provisional account is tested against new conditions (paragraph 4); the final inheritance supplies observations and questions for the next shoreline test (paragraph 8). Both make later checking possible. Neither turns longer records into certainty, freezes the revised estimate, or requires a different method before existing conclusions may be reconsidered.

items.answerText: a rigid image of serious rehearsal toward a more flexible understanding of musical work
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 1 makes seriousness a picture of chairs and windows; paragraph 8 preserves the goal of playing well while relaxing exclusivity. The change is toward a more flexible understanding of musical work. The narrator does not end by seeking fewer interruptions, adopting the aunt as director, or rejecting preparation: the quartet still works through its planned repairs and adapts useful suggestions.

items.answerText: The aunt plays it during Sunday visits
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 2 gives the mother’s reason: the aunt likes to play after Sunday lunch. No quartet member plays it. The later musical exchange does not make tuning, a future piano part, or the chair arrangement the original reason for leaving it in place. Distinguish a stated motive from later possible uses.

items.answerText: Describes a difficult measure rather than the room’s appearance
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 7 explicitly contrasts telling the aunt about the stubborn third measure with describing chairs and windows. This action demonstrates attention to the music itself. The aunt then asks to see the score; the narrator does not start by revisiting the room arrangement, requesting the earlier song, or listing the mother’s conditions.

items.answerText: enjoys an unexpected musical exchange while worrying about the planned rehearsal time
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 4 states simultaneous enjoyment and resentment: the exchange is appealing, but the quartet has only an hour and a list of repairs. It is not said to fix the third measure, replace the rehearsal, or be imposed by the aunt. Lina invites the opening to be repeated, and the planned work follows afterward.

items.answerText: became less rigid
items.reviewedEvidence: The subject of “loosened” is the conviction that serious work requires exclusivity. The narrator still wants to play well, but that conviction becomes less rigid. Improved playing does not make seriousness unimportant, and the ending does not install a new absolute rule. Use both the sentence’s subject and the preceding statement of continuing ambition.

items.answerText: challenge the narrator to distinguish a useful setup from an impressive-looking one
items.reviewedEvidence: The question asks whether the arrangement should help the players or merely look like rehearsal. Moving stands then gives Lina a workable sightline and improves the sound. It challenges appearance as the priority; it does not ask Lina to endure the setup, elevate room restoration above music, or endorse the photographs’ arrangement.

items.answerText: a concrete reminder that the room already accommodates changing uses
items.reviewedEvidence: In paragraph 6 the narrator sees old dents while returning chairs and realizes the room already contains many arrangements. The physical detail makes earlier uses visible. It does not date the quartet’s occupancy, predict comfort, or directly explain musical improvement; its function is to revise the narrator’s claim to a wholly new, dedicated room.

items.answerText: Both reveal that improvement involves trying and adjusting a passage
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 5 shows several attempts at the same difficult measures; paragraph 7 shows the aunt repeat a phrase and adjust her touch. The narrator recognizes the resemblance: trying and revising are musical work in either setting. Difficulty remains, the aunt adjusts her own playing, and neither scene requires discarding the written music.

items.answerText: Returning the chairs willingly shows acceptance of the room’s other purposes
items.reviewedEvidence: Compare paragraph 6’s resistance with paragraph 8’s unprompted return of the chairs. The narrator accepts that serious rehearsal can coexist with the room’s other purposes. The group still pursues improvement, modifies the aunt’s suggestion, and organizes its own work; the action does not transfer authority or reject planning.

items.answerText: evaluates a narrower service change while keeping its evidence and limitations clear
items.reviewedEvidence: The whole passage evaluates the return-only window, checking denominators, reminders and seasonality, purchasing limits, and volunteer labor. That supports the key’s account of a limited service change evaluated with clear evidence and limits. The collection’s required size is not compared experimentally; the window’s separate effect remains unresolved; and the purchasing question is one boundary of the trial, not the investigation the library proceeds to carry out.

items.answerText: Preparing a tool for a new borrower requires more volunteers
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 2 states the staffing difference: checking equipment for a new borrower needs more volunteers than receiving a return. Earlier returns can leave time for later inspection, but the window does not promise to accept only inspection-free items. Member daylight preferences and replacement purchases are not the reason given for withholding new loans.

items.answerText: One tool returned by its due date
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 3 defines the unit as a tool returned by its due date. A borrower returning three tools contributes three returns, not one. A scheduled return can be late, and an on-time return does not itself guarantee the tool passes inspection and becomes available the next Saturday. Follow the definition rather than the hoped-for downstream effect.

items.answerText: distinguishes evidence about circulation from evidence about the range of tools needed
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 6 separates blocked requests for tools still out from unmet demand for tools never owned and demand during the repair workshop. Circulation data do not describe the collection’s required range. Better returns need not be solved first, and the seasonal change neither proves reduced demand overall nor justifies fewer purchases.

items.answerText: a process by which the change could produce an effect
items.reviewedEvidence: The surrounding sentence concerns how an earlier return could allow inspection and then a Saturday loan. That is a process capable of producing an effect—a mechanism. Definitions, an isolated statistical pattern, and the final policy combination are different concepts. The coordinator also says a plausible process does not substitute for evidence separating causes.

items.answerText: staffing must also make the service feasible
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 7 links the door image to whether volunteers can actually staff the service. A favorable percentage cannot itself supply that labor. The passage includes staffing beside the table rather than treating comments as stronger outcome evidence or replacing the return measure. Saturday time savings are not what the phrase emphasizes.

items.answerText: reduce one source of ambiguity in interpreting the window’s effect
items.reviewedEvidence: If reminder practices remain consistent, one simultaneous change is less able to explain a later difference attributed to the window. That is a reduction in causal ambiguity, not a guarantee of identical seasons or a method for identifying each person’s motive. The recommendation addresses the confound, not simply a raw-count pattern.

items.answerText: 90 percent
items.reviewedEvidence: The requested fraction uses on-time tools over scheduled tools in the same trial period: 81/90 = 0.90, or 90%. Eighty-one is a count, not a percentage; 75% is the earlier period’s 60/80; and 21 is the increase in the raw on-time count, 81 − 60. Identify both the unit and denominator before calculating.

items.answerText: Unfilled requests due to tools remaining out decreased during the combined trial changes
items.reviewedEvidence: The table directly shows requests blocked by tools still out falling 18→9 during the combined changes. It does not count all kinds of unmet demand, identify individual borrowers, or separate reminders from the window. A supported description can report the fall without converting it into an overall fulfillment rate or a single-cause finding.

items.answerText: useful restoration should preserve access to evidence and make the choices behind processing visible
items.reviewedEvidence: Passage A offers processed and unprocessed copies with notes; Passage B supports that choice so later researchers can ask different questions. The shared claim is accessible restoration with inspectable decisions and preserved evidence. Neither ranks audience sounds below music for every inquiry, treats notes as a substitute for the source, or turns uncertain sound classification into an absolute rule.

items.answerText: Leaves the sound and documents the uncertainty
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 2 says the engineer leaves an uncertain sound in place and describes the uncertainty. There is no complete acoustic reference (paragraph 1). The transcript handles uncertain words in paragraph 3, not a rule allowing automatic smoothing. Preserving the unprocessed file also does not mean every doubtful sound is removed from the listening version.

items.answerText: To illustrate a detail that could matter to a different research question
items.reviewedEvidence: In paragraphs 5–6, shifting chairs might distract someone studying vocal technique yet matter to someone studying the concert as a social occasion. The example makes relevance depend on the inquiry. It does not allow an audience count, isolate a microphone defect, or establish that social history outranks musical research.

items.answerText: discards the unprocessed file after producing an attractive listening copy
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 7 names the concern: keeping only the polished result would force future researchers to depend on today’s choices. The historian supports accessible processed versions and notes, so neither a singer-focused listening copy nor uncertainty documentation is objectionable. What matters is retaining the alternative evidence for reconsideration.

items.answerText: relevant to the inquiry
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 6 contrasts “irrelevant to one inquiry” with “pertinent to another.” The opposing context gives “relevant to the inquiry.” A sound can be relevant even if its source is uncertain or its acoustic measurement limited; pertinence does not itself certify authenticity, sequence, or measurability.

items.answerText: illustrate why different kinds of sound call for different restoration judgments
items.reviewedEvidence: A known surface click and possibly authentic vocal texture have different origins, so smoothing them involves different judgments. Paragraph 2 then addresses cases where the distinction is uncertain. The point is neither an infallible automatic rule nor ranking defects; removing one click cannot reconstruct the complete acoustic reference paragraph 1 says is unavailable.

items.answerText: explains why current listening goals should not determine all material retained for future use
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 8 distinguishes a selection for today’s encounter from keeping evidence for future encounters not yet known. This explains retaining more than the present listening copy. Notes alone cannot replace a discarded source, and preservation does not require the public presentation to reproduce every sound without selection. The responsibilities are related, not interchangeable.

items.answerText: A processed copy can help listeners, while an alternative copy and notes allow decisions to be reconsidered
items.reviewedEvidence: The engineer supplies two versions and documentation in paragraph 3; the historian explicitly endorses that approach in paragraph 7. It combines accessibility with the ability to reconsider decisions. Transcripts do not retain all sound evidence, future questions need not match current goals, and the engineer retains sounds whose origin is uncertain rather than automatically removing them.

items.answerText: By emphasizing that later inquiries may value details that current listeners find distracting
items.reviewedEvidence: Passage A explains intervention and uncertainty in making a listening version. Passage B adds why retaining alternatives matters over time: a distracting chair sound can answer a later social-history question. Classifying clicks versus roughness is already the engineer’s concern; the historian neither proposes a new recording nor tells future scholars to prefer the processed file.

items.answerText: how researchers use root images to investigate growth while examining the method’s limits
items.reviewedEvidence: The repeated images enable investigation, but the passage also checks tube disturbance, inference about individuals, seasonal confounds, and tracing disagreement. The key captures both the method and the examination of its limits. Intact redistribution is explicitly rejected, rainfall is not yet isolated, and tracing improvement is one part rather than the passage’s whole subject.

items.answerText: To compare visible root length at consistent locations
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 2 explains that consistent positions make later and earlier visible-root lengths comparable at the same location. The method does not follow every connection to a parent plant or make installation effects equal. Camera position still must be consistent; omitting it would undermine the very comparison the repeated sections permit.

items.answerText: Creates shared examples and confidence labels, then repeats some tracing
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 6 describes shared example images, confidence labels, and another tracing exercise after practice. These make the counting rule more consistent while leaving ambiguity visible. The team does not designate one tracer as correct, choose the larger estimate, or assume software removes the need for judgment.

items.answerText: test moisture’s contribution more directly than the seasonal association permits
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 5 first identifies moisture, temperature, and season as changing together, then proposes extra water under otherwise similar conditions. This is a more direct test of moisture’s contribution. Checking that treatment changes underground moisture verifies the intervention; it does not make the experiment primarily a rainfall survey or a tube-age test.

items.answerText: not influencing the process being observed
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 4 asks whether installing a tube leaves a gap or alters water travel. A “neutral” boundary would not itself influence the growth being observed. “Representative,” “unchanged,” and “equally visible” are different properties: a stable, easily photographed boundary could still alter local growth.

items.answerText: contrast an appealing broad claim with the narrower evidence the images provide
items.reviewedEvidence: The visitor turns a local pattern into a claim about every plant moving its root system. The researchers then explain what the images can show: new visible growth and disappearing traces at selected sites. The contrast clarifies an inference limit; it does not introduce the deeper observations, connect all roots to plants, or deny any drought-related response.

items.answerText: prevent a memorable illustration from being mistaken for the broader results
items.reviewedEvidence: Paragraph 7 says the sequence illustrates change but cannot substitute for results across plots. Clarity can make a picture memorable without making its response representative. The caption therefore prevents overgeneralization; it does not certify a most-common case, an undisturbed control tube, or priority over the broader summary.

items.answerText: Both examine how the observation method may shape the reported results
items.reviewedEvidence: The tube-age comparison checks a physical effect introduced by observation: installation may alter soil. The tracing exercise checks a classification effect: people may assign different lengths to faint marks. Both ask how the method shapes the reported result. Neither is a complete independent root measurement or simply a comparison of plant age and season.

items.answerText: Repeated imaging is useful, but its interpretations should be tested within the comparisons and limitations it supports
items.reviewedEvidence: The final paragraph values repeated views while asking which comparisons they support, which influences they introduce, and how another method could test an interpretation. Earlier examples supply those limits. Standardized tracing does not reveal every root, a watering test does not erase tube disturbance, and the passage does not require abandoning a useful method before reporting qualified findings.

displayChoicePolicy.scope: All Reading questions rendered through the shared QuestionView: focused practice, daily study, timed sections and saved review.
displayChoicePolicy.method: A deterministic question-ID-seeded permutation controls display positions only. Clicks, selections, eliminations, saved records and grading retain canonical content indices. Feedback converts canonical choices back into the same displayed letters.
displayChoicePolicy.compatibility: No content keys or storage formats change. The same question has the same displayed order after reload and in review. Previously saved canonical answers still resolve to the same answer text and correctness; display labels reflect the current fixed display policy.
displayChoicePolicy.verification: Five regression tests cover invertibility over the full question bank, stable reload, both forms losing the repeating position cue, actual button callbacks into drill/section persistence, elimination/deselection and matching feedback letters.

formativeReview.scope: All 42 Reading and 43 Science lesson activities were read with their prompts, source excerpts and feedback. Activities remain guided applications between teaching and independent practice.
formativeReview.changes: Replace obviously unrelated alternatives with plausible local meanings, changed scope, source-unit mistakes, confounds, causal overreach, or arithmetic/model errors. Preserve section positions, answer indices and correct-answer text. Clarify the dilution-factor definition, equal water volumes in a controlled comparison, the scope of a summary prompt, and a necessity-versus-sufficiency task.

items.answerText: Temperature (°C)

Removal is 50−20 = 30 mg/L. Divide by the initial 50, not the remaining 20: 30/50 = 60%.

items.answerText: Sample M

items.answerText: Pool U

items.answerText: 20 organisms/h

items.answerText: 4 mg/L
items.reviewedEvidence: Mass flow is 12×2+4×10 = 64 mg/s. Water flow is 16 L/s. The flow-weighted concentration is 64/16 = 4 mg/L.

items.answerText: 40 mg/L
items.reviewedEvidence: A fivefold dilution leaves one-fifth of the original concentration, so undo it with 8×5 = 40 mg/L. Dividing by 5 gives 1.6 and dilutes again; adding 5 gives 13 and treats a factor as an amount; leaving 8 unchanged ignores the dilution.

items.answerText: 0–2 min

The second total drop is larger, but it takes three times as long. Falling in both intervals does not make the rates equal, and average rates can be compared without instantaneous measurements.
Seven minutes is halfway from 5 to 9 min, so use the midpoint of 46 and 34: (46+34)/2 = 40°C.

items.answerText: Dose 3 has the largest measured response
items.reviewedEvidence: Among the three measured outputs, 11 at dose 3 is largest. The fall to 8 at dose 5 contradicts a continuously increasing claim. No measurements locate an exact overall optimum or establish a straight-line value of 9.5 at dose 4; those add claims beyond the observations.
The coefficient of d is the slope: each additional meter lowers temperature by 3°C. The 18°C intercept is the value at zero depth.

items.answerText: 12 mm

The selected series rises to 10 and then falls to 6, so its direction reverses. Smaller positive increases alone do not create a turning point.

items.answerText: The modeled relationship continues beyond the tested range
items.reviewedEvidence: Eighteen lies outside the validated 2–12 mg/L range, so the existing model is being extrapolated. Its use requires assuming the modeled relationship remains applicable there. The data do not instead require a new linear rule, a constant boundary value, or an output restricted to the observed range.

items.answerText: The same oil without the drug
items.reviewedEvidence: An oil-only control holds the carrier constant. Comparing against no oil changes both drug presence and carrier presence.

items.answerText: Use the same water amount in both groups
items.reviewedEvidence: Heating and water amount currently vary together. Giving both groups the same water isolates heating. More measurements, more heated pots, or a more precise thermometer can improve sampling or precision while leaving the water confound intact.

items.answerText: Equal masses and water temperatures; stirred versus unstirred
items.reviewedEvidence: Compare stirred and unstirred cups at the same solid mass and water temperature. Equal water volumes and a shared endpoint complete the control. Changing temperature or mass with stirring mixes causes, while two stirred cups do not test stirring at all.
Treatment was assigned to trays, so the independent units are the three trays. More seedlings improve sampling within a tray but do not create more treatment assignments.

items.answerText: Assign some animals B before A
items.reviewedEvidence: Counterbalancing A→B and B→A makes treatment order vary rather than remain tied to treatment identity. Repeating or measuring the same fixed sequence more closely does not test the alternative order. Persistent carryover can still require fresh groups even after a simple order effect is tested.

items.answerText: Its measured effect depends on temperature
items.reviewedEvidence: The treatment-minus-control effect is 2 units at 10°C and 8 at 30°C, so it depends on the tested temperature. Those effects do not state how untreated values change. The effect is positive at both temperatures and becomes four times, not three times, as large; a mechanism or untested pattern is not established.

items.answerText: Use a ruler with finer graduations
items.reviewedEvidence: Finer graduations directly improve resolution of the expected 0.2 cm difference. Repetition or more samples does not give an individual reading finer marks. Calibration addresses systematic accuracy, but a calibrated ruler with the same coarse graduations still has the stated resolution limit.

items.answerText: Bubbles are visible
items.reviewedEvidence: Both mechanisms can produce visible bubbles. Their chemical source, not the presence of bubbles, is the disagreement.

items.answerText: Oxygen supply changed along with the chemical process
items.reviewedEvidence: The manipulation changes both a chemical process and oxygen delivery, each relevant to a competing explanation. The fall in light output therefore cannot be assigned uniquely to either. Repeating that confounded manipulation does not separate them; a control preserving oxygen delivery while inhibiting the chemical would be more informative.

items.answerText: Both routes remain possible
items.reviewedEvidence: Survival demonstrates that either process could deliver fragments. Evidence about the particular deposit is still required to choose its actual history.

items.answerText: Same light, different humidity
items.reviewedEvidence: Hold light fixed and change humidity so that a response difference targets humidity. Changing both factors mixes the predictions.

items.answerText: B

Both predict 6 at A; measuring that shared prediction more precisely does not separate them. A model need not first be shown correct at all settings before an informative test is possible.

items.answerText: The nondetection cannot resolve the prediction
items.reviewedEvidence: The predicted 0.4 is below the 1-unit detection limit. Both zero and 0.4 would be undetected, so this result cannot distinguish those possibilities. It neither contradicts the subthreshold prediction nor confirms its exact magnitude.

items.answerText: Dry soil is necessary
items.reviewedEvidence: Germination in wet soil is a counterexample to dry soil being necessary. Warmth is present, so its necessity is not contradicted. A result under a different set of conditions also does not disprove that dry soil alone, or warm dry soil, could be sufficient; necessity and sufficiency are distinct claims.

items.answerText: A reproducible mismatch at 22°C
items.reviewedEvidence: Twenty-two degrees lies within the stated domain and holds the modeled material fixed. The other choices test an unsupported extension.

items.answerText: It halves
items.reviewedEvidence: The length change gives ×2 and the area change gives ÷4. Together, 2/4 = 1/2, with k held constant.

items.reviewedEvidence: Subtract background from each reading: 255−5 = 250 and 130−5 = 125. The corrected signal halves. Halving the initial raw reading gives 127.5 rather than the observed corrected value; adding background gives 260 and 135; leaving both raw values unchanged omits the correction.
Divide by C: q = 8/(3/C+1). The 3/C term approaches zero, so q approaches 8 from below.

items.answerText: The model needs revision despite its first success
items.reviewedEvidence: Both experiments are reliable and satisfy the stated conditions, so the second contradiction requires revision despite the first success. Omitting a contradictory in-scope test does not repair the claim. A competing model must also face both datasets; fitting one does not automatically establish a fit to the other.

items.answerText: It decreases tenfold

items.answerText: Its charge, while its element stays the same

items.answerText: 6 g/cm³

Net production equals gross minus consumption. Add back the 4 consumed: gross = 9+4 = 13 units per hour.

items.answerText: The 100 g sample, by twice as much
items.reviewedEvidence: With Q and c fixed, ΔT = Q/(mc), so the 100 g sample warms twice as much as the 200 g sample. Equal supplied heat is not equal temperature rise, and equal specific heat does not mean equal heat capacity: total heat per degree also depends on mass.

items.answerText: It stays 30%
items.reviewedEvidence: Counts become 60 and 140. The fraction remains 60/200 = 30%; equal multiplication preserves proportions.

items.answerText: 30 m/s
items.reviewedEvidence: Multiply frequency by wavelength: 5 cycles/s × 6 m/cycle = 30 m/s. The cycle unit cancels.

items.answerText: Erosion
items.reviewedEvidence: The fragments are already loose and are moving downstream, so erosion is the relevant process. Weathering breaks material down in place; deposition settles transported sediment; dissolution produces dissolved material rather than describing transport of the existing solid fragments.

items.answerText: An accurate but limited label is expanded and reorganized to show another kind of value
items.reviewedEvidence: The storage description remains because it is accurate. The curator adds relationship and exchange, then moves that material higher while retaining limits on the account.

items.answerText: Longer hours show promise but require financial review
items.reviewedEvidence: Keep both parts: more attendance makes the pilot promising, while unexpectedly high staffing costs leave sustainability unresolved. A benefit does not establish that the costs are justified, and the passage already reports the attendance rise; that is not what the budget review must discover.

items.answerText: The curator discovers a different purpose for the map
items.reviewedEvidence: The curator changes the question used to judge the map: it records memories rather than geographic distances. The map does not become a substitute for measured distances, and the passage gives no rule linking accuracy to the number of memories. Summarize the change in understanding, not a new fact about the object.

items.answerText: Weekend trips increased
items.reviewedEvidence: “Weekend trips increased” gives only a benefit and omits the unresolved costs. Both other summaries include an access gain and a financial qualification, so they can cover the whole argument. A detail can be accurate yet too narrow to serve as the main idea.

items.answerText: Dismissal becomes engagement
items.reviewedEvidence: The opening dismissal and final act of writing support a change toward engagement. Writing at the desk is more than treating it only as an archival record. Nothing compares the quality of her work with the unfinished drafts, so superiority would require an added assumption.

items.answerText: Ivo still checks time for his bus, but watches his work more closely
items.reviewedEvidence: The bus detail rules out rejecting schedules. The contrast between bus time and workshop attention supports using different measures for different tasks.

items.answerText: Sofia keeps measurements while specifying where tasting and judgment are needed
items.reviewedEvidence: The quantity remains a useful starting point while the card states where judgment belongs. That combines measurement and tasting rather than replacing either. Making the number override later tasting reverses the qualification, while keeping the instructions unchanged misses how the written guidance has been clarified.

items.answerText: The comparison between volunteers’ notes and the time-stamped log
items.reviewedEvidence: The question asks for a requested action. The final sentence names that action; the other details describe the study but do not answer what was requested.

items.answerText: The time phrase attached to surveyed
items.reviewedEvidence: The question asks when, so locate the time condition attached to the action “surveyed”: after the evening service ended. The team identifies the actor and riders identifies the respondents; neither tells when the survey happened.

items.answerText: The increase followed the repair
items.reviewedEvidence: Sequence is stated; cause is not isolated. The changed counting route is another possible explanation.

items.answerText: Ninety tools were returned
items.reviewedEvidence: Returns count tools, not unique borrowers. Keep the number attached to its unit.

items.answerText: The result offers tentative support
items.reviewedEvidence: “Suggestive” offers tentative support, and the small sample limits how firm the conclusion can be. Calling the evidence conclusive drops the qualification; saying it supplies no support drops its positive force. A faithful paraphrase preserves both direction and degree of certainty.

items.answerText: The librarian asked about after-school use, so the office added sessions that recorded older children
items.reviewedEvidence: The librarian’s question comes before the new observations. The choice reverses the order and turns the later result into the reason for collecting it.

items.answerText: “the figures could overlap”
items.reviewedEvidence: “Could overlap” explicitly means the same visit can contribute to both figures. Clearer labels and understanding explain context but do not state the counting relationship as directly.

items.answerText: He wants to give the next borrower a useful technique to try
items.reviewedEvidence: The note offers softly started notes as something the next borrower might try. That modest practical purpose follows from the action. A universal preference contradicts the explicit limit, and prescribing a technique for everyone turns an invitation to experiment into a rule.

items.answerText: She wanted to prevent recordings from being confused
items.reviewedEvidence: Labeling each file before making another most directly supports avoiding confusion among recordings. Revising interview answers and selecting material for publication are possible later tasks, but neither is indicated by the action. Prefer the motive requiring the least added information.

items.answerText: The historian wanted to confirm access
items.reviewedEvidence: Checking opening hours is a direct step toward confirming access before travel. It does not establish that a particular document is available or that a special appointment has been arranged. Those claims add different information the action does not supply.

items.answerText: Interest with concern about sustainability
items.reviewedEvidence: “Clever” supports interest, while the question about maintenance after the grant expresses a sustainability concern. Confidence that funding continues reverses that concern. Doubt about originality also misplaces the reservation: he praises the idea but asks who will keep it working.

items.answerText: Every resident supported the change
items.reviewedEvidence: “Others remained skeptical” directly conflicts with universal support. Use explicit counterevidence to eliminate an attractive overstatement.

items.answerText: He asks to keep the pencil lines around the unfinished tile
items.reviewedEvidence: His request retains the portrait’s focus on work rather than trophies. It is an action supporting acceptance; his earlier comment about the cabinet expresses a reservation.

items.answerText: He values the side path’s encounters while still using the front steps for quick errands
items.reviewedEvidence: The paragraph explicitly keeps the front entrance useful and the side path longer. Luis sometimes chooses the side path alone because his experience of it has changed.

items.answerText: indications that can guide further investigation
items.reviewedEvidence: The researchers retain the photographs but seek consistent observations. “Clues” preserves their limited value without treating them as either proof or useless records.

items.answerText: Carefully considering
items.reviewedEvidence: Substitute each meaning into “After weighing the costs.” The committee considers the costs before choosing a trial; it is not necessarily calculating an exact total or changing the expenses. The phrase describes evaluation leading to a decision.

items.answerText: Minimal
items.reviewedEvidence: The ornate design is contrasted with a revision using only two lines, which makes “minimal” the local meaning. “Extra” and “available if needed” are real senses of spare, but neither explains the contrast in ornamentation. Context selects among valid dictionary senses.

items.answerText: The uncertainty persistently troubled the work
items.reviewedEvidence: “Haunted” gives the unanswered question a persistent, troubling presence during the project. A useful focus removes that negative pressure, while a return only after completion changes the timing. Preserve both the emotional force and continuing influence of the figurative verb.

items.answerText: Cautious
items.reviewedEvidence: The report actually states its conclusion and acknowledges an improvement, so it is neither withheld nor wholly skeptical. Its remaining uncertainty limits confidence in that improvement. “Cautious” preserves this balanced stance.

items.answerText: She restores the specific image of a stone bridge
items.reviewedEvidence: The specific bridge image is the stated remedy for becoming “unmoored.” That contrast points to a lack of concrete grounding, rather than a literal detached boat.

items.answerText: the greeting’s role in this story
items.reviewedEvidence: The translator wants to preserve what the greeting accomplishes between characters. The phrase concerns its function in the story, not hours of labor or grammar alone.

items.answerText: It introduces an assumption that the comparison exercise will test
items.reviewedEvidence: The instructor responds to Ben’s assumption by asking him to compare the actual shadow with black paint. The sentence sets up a belief for examination.

items.answerText: Provide a concrete illustration of the claim
items.reviewedEvidence: The resident’s commute makes the general access problem concrete. One example illustrates the claim without proving a unique cause for every commuter. Because the described difficulty matches rather than contradicts the broad claim, it does not function as counterevidence.

items.answerText: Cautiously favorable
items.reviewedEvidence: “Useful relief” supplies approval; “long-term costs remain uncertain” qualifies it. Cautiously favorable preserves both parts. Unreserved approval drops the cost concern, while skepticism about any relief ignores the explicitly stated benefit.

items.answerText: To introduce a concern the writer addresses
items.reviewedEvidence: The writer introduces a concern and then addresses it with data. That sequence distinguishes presenting an opposing position from adopting it. Nothing establishes shared interpretation of the data; the quotation sets up the response rather than supplying the writer’s own evidence.

items.answerText: A feeling of warmth and shelter
items.reviewedEvidence: Hearths associate the glowing windows with warmth and shelter against the rain. The comparison shapes atmosphere; it does not establish literal indoor fireplaces. Isolation from other homes and an obstructed view are not features supplied by the image.

items.answerText: It distinguishes the visible pattern from the practical reasons that produce it
items.reviewedEvidence: The grower accepts that rows look tidy, then explains decisions about equipment, slopes, and frost. “Neatness is a result” distinguishes an appearance from its practical causes. It does not deny the visible order or prescribe one fixed grid independent of local conditions.

items.answerText: Hopeful about its promise but careful about the claim’s scope
items.reviewedEvidence: The teacher retains the garden’s promise and asks for claims proportionate to observations. Both the support and the caution are explicit.

items.answerText: Both support protecting the ground, while the advocate also insists that access be an explicit study goal
items.reviewedEvidence: Both accept environmental protection. The advocate adds a condition about the study’s aim; neither writer calls for immediate widening without investigation.

items.answerText: They share an aim but differ over a condition
items.reviewedEvidence: Both favor improved access through longer hours, but B explicitly makes support conditional on staffing funds. That is a shared aim with a distinct condition. A does not state the same funding assumption, and neither source disputes whether access is the aim.

items.answerText: It improved access, while its costs need evaluation
items.reviewedEvidence: An access gain and uncertain costs can both be true. Combine them without turning a benefit into a financial verdict or treating the cost qualification as evidence that access did not improve. Each source contributes a different part of the assessment.

items.answerText: No: the units measure different things
items.reviewedEvidence: Seat occupancy and distinct visitors use different counting units. The same person can occupy a seat at several observations, and the same seating area does not prevent repeated counting. Consistent locations help compare occupancy; they do not convert it into a unique-person count.

items.answerText: Improvement occurred in the two tested groups
items.reviewedEvidence: Both tested groups improved, so the combined conclusion can name those two groups. The statements do not give effect sizes or establish that age has no influence. Two positive directions do not imply equal magnitudes or an absence of differences across ages.

items.answerText: Crossings can exceed unique visitors, but a correction needs observed travel patterns
items.reviewedEvidence: The device counts crossings, including returns, while volunteers try to count distinct people. A difference need not mean volunteers missed people. Some visitors cross twice and others use another exit, so an automatic divide-by-two rule is also unsupported. A correction needs observations of those travel patterns.

items.answerText: Some measures improved, but averages, disruptive peaks, and the cause of change remain distinct questions
items.reviewedEvidence: One average rose, interviews describe disruptive peaks, and nearby construction changed routes. The combined claim must retain differences among measures and uncertainty about cause.
